# The Prime Wavelet Tree

Code and data for compressing the table of Carmichael numbers below 10<sup>24</sup> with the prime wavelet tree. Paper: *The Prime Wavelet Tree: Compressing the Carmichael Numbers*, by Ankur Gupta, Jonathan Webster and Sylvia Webster (Butler University). Submitted to DCC 2027.

- **Repository:** [github.com/ankurgupta-cs/prime-wavelet-tree](https://github.com/ankurgupta-cs/prime-wavelet-tree)
- **Website:** [ankurgupta-cs.github.io/prime-wavelet-tree](https://ankurgupta-cs.github.io/prime-wavelet-tree/)
- **Data:** [blue.butler.edu/~jewebste/prime-wavelet-tree](https://blue.butler.edu/~jewebste/prime-wavelet-tree/)
- **Paper:** [arXiv:2610.02550](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02550)
- **Citation:** [BibTeX on the website](https://ankurgupta-cs.github.io/prime-wavelet-tree/#cite)
- **Licence:** data public domain ([CC0 1.0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/)), code licence pending a decision by Butler University

The [website](https://ankurgupta-cs.github.io/prime-wavelet-tree/) has the results table, every data file with its SHA-256, and the commands that rebuild and check each file.
<!-- links:end -->

The paper stores the table of all Carmichael numbers below 10<sup>24</sup>, computed by A. Shallue and J. Webster, in eight ways. These are the eight cells of its A/B/C matrix (Table 2). One more file uses heuristically chosen divisors. This repository holds the code that wrote those files, the commands that rebuild, decode and check each one, and the logs of the runs behind every number in the table.

Three on/off switches define the cells, and a cell's tag gives them in the order A, B, C. Switch A stores the divisor d<sub>min</sub>(n), from which n follows, instead of n. Switch B stores each prime set as a path in a prime wavelet tree (PWT) instead of storing numbers in a sorted list. Switch C codes the values with residue classes or entropy coding instead of one byte-aligned VByte code each. So cell 000 is the sorted list of n in VByte, and cell 111 is the coded tree over d<sub>min</sub>.

Each file is lossless. Decoding it gives back every Carmichael number (CN). Every file has been compared, number by number, with the oracle, a binary copy of the original table.

N = 308,279,939 Carmichael numbers (CNs). Times are single-threaded minutes on an Intel Core i9-9900K (8 cores, 16 threads), 64 GB RAM, NVMe SSD, Windows 10, except where noted.

- [a] The factoring part is scaled from the measured per-number cost on 3,084,288 CNs (every 100th oracle block). Every factorization was also checked against the oracle.
- [b] The d<sub>min</sub> list itself decodes in 0.03 (100) and 0.61 (101) minutes. The rest is factoring every d.
- [c] As run, with 15 threads for the extraction, 6 for the search and 4 for encoding. The search alone took 119,102 s (33.1 h). The file stores the chosen divisors, so it can be rebuilt without repeating the search. That rebuild takes about 13 min. Exporting the stored paths takes 5.1 min on one thread, and encoding them takes 7.5 min on 4 threads.
- Certify decodes the file and compares every CN with the oracle. The trees were certified on 2026-09-26 on an otherwise idle machine. Cell 101 was certified on 2026-08-19 on an otherwise idle machine. Cells 000, 001 and 100 were certified on 2026-10-06 while other jobs ran.
<!-- table:end -->

The same table, with definitions and sources, is in [COMPARISON.pdf](COMPARISON.pdf). Every number in it is typed once, in [results/cells.tsv](results/cells.tsv). `make table` renders this README table, the per-cell manifests `cells/*/CELL`, `SHA256SUMS` and `results/comparison.tex` from it. `make site` renders the website in `docs/` from the same file.

`make fetch-CELL` downloads a file into `data/` and checks its size and SHA-256. `SHA256SUMS` here is the same file as in the data folder. To check downloads by hand, run `cd data && sha256sum -c --ignore-missing ../SHA256SUMS`.

The four **C = 0 cells** (000, 100, 010, 110) store one VByte per value or symbol. They are not hosted. Each one is rebuilt from the oracle with `make rebuild-CELL`, which must reproduce the hash in its manifest (see below).

## Quick start

```sh
make                      # build the tools into build/ (C++20, no other dependencies, tested with GCC 16.1.0 on Windows)
make test                 # unit tests
make check                # self-test: every encoder and decoder on the 8,241 CNs below 10^12

make fetch-111 verify-111 # download data/carmichael-1e24-cell111-pwt-dmin.pwt2, check size, SHA-256 and structure
make fetch-oracle         # download the oracle, data/carmichael-1e24-oracle.orc1
make certify-111          # decode and compare every CN with the oracle
make rebuild-111          # rebuild the file from the oracle, byte for byte
make verify-hosted        # verify the five hosted cell files and the oracle
```

`CELL` is one of `000 001 100 101 010 011 110 111 111x`. `111x` is the PWT + d\* row. Other targets are `decode-CELL` (write the decoded CNs to `work/`), `paths-CELL` (export a tree's stored paths), `verify-oracle`, `rebuild-oracle` (from the text, with `make fetch-text`) and `search-dstar`.

Environment: `DATA` (downloaded files, default `data/`), `WORK` (intermediates and rebuilt files, default `work/`), `ORC1` (the oracle, default `$DATA/carmichael-1e24-oracle.orc1`), `THREADS`, `BIN` (default `build/`). Large files never belong in the repository. Git ignores `data/` and `work/`.

What each check proves:

- **verify** (minutes): the file has the published bytes and decodes. For the trees and the lists of n, the decoded set hashes to the CN set's SHA-256. For the d<sub>min</sub> lists, it hashes to the d<sub>min</sub> list's.
- **certify** (2 to 4 minutes for a tree, 1 to 2 minutes for a list of n, about 25 minutes on 13 threads for a d<sub>min</sub> list, which needs every d factored): every decoded CN equals the oracle's, in order.
- **rebuild** (the Build column, plus disk for the intermediates, `disk_gb` in each `CELL`): the encoders write the published file from the oracle, byte for byte.
- **check** (about a minute): all of the above on the 8,241 CNs below 10<sup>12</sup>, against frozen hashes in `tests/prefix/golden_prefix.tsv`.

## How the C = 0 cells are rebuilt

Each `cells/<cell>/build.sh` runs two steps. An extraction writes a shared intermediate from the oracle into `work/`. Then the encoder writes the file. The intermediates and their hashes are listed in `results/INTERMEDIATES`.

| Cell | Extraction (oracle to intermediate) | Encode |
|---|---|---|
| 000 | `nstats_orc1 ORC1 --emit-n n.raw --emit-only` | `list_build vbyte n.raw c000-n-vbyte.vbg` |
| 100 | `dlist_from_paths --orc1 ORC1 d.raw` (the d<sub>min</sub> search) | `list_build vbyte d.raw c100-dmin-vbyte.vbg` |
| 010 | `trie_paths ORC1 fpaths.bin --full --fields 14` | `pwt2_encode fpaths.bin ORC1 c010-pwt-full-bytes.pwt2n --fields 14 --full --naive` |
| 110 | `trie_paths ORC1 dpaths.bin --fields 12` (the d<sub>min</sub> search) | `pwt2_encode dpaths.bin ORC1 c110-pwt-dmin-bytes.pwt2n --fields 12 --naive` |

The C = 1 cells use the same extractions. Cell 001 is `list_build classes n.raw ... --mod 10810800 --targets-self`. Cell 101 is `list_build classes d.raw ... --mod 2310 --targets-orc1 ORC1`, and `cnd_encode` writes the same bytes. Cells 011 and 111 are `pwt2_encode` with `--ctx-set 3` in place of `--naive`. Thread counts change only the time, never the bytes.

## The PWT + d\* file

The d\* divisors come from a 33-hour greedy local search (`dsel_set2`). It moves each CN, in turn, to the divisor whose path is cheapest given all the others. This is a heuristic, not a minimum. The PWT + d\* file stores the chosen divisors, so it can be rebuilt without repeating the search. `cells/111x-pwt-dstar/build.sh` has two routes (`ROUTE=`).

- **paths** (default): `pwt2_decode --emit-paths` exports the divisors stored in the d\* file, and `pwt2_encode` re-encodes them to the same bytes. This route was run on the full table. The exported paths are the search's output as a set (same records, tree order). They re-encode to the published file byte for byte.
- **search**: rerun the search with its logged command lines (`make search-dstar`, about 33 hours on 6 threads and 16 GB RAM). This route has not been rerun. The published search ran once (2026-09-24 to 26) with an earlier build of `dsel_set2`, whose header `pwt2.hpp` has changed since. It prices candidates in floating point. So a rerun is not known to reproduce the published choice byte for byte.

The search writes its choice as one mask per CN (`--masks-out`, [docs/MASKS_FORMAT.md](docs/MASKS_FORMAT.md)). `ROUTE=masks` encodes the file from such masks. The masks of the published search are not hosted. Their SHA-256 is `masks_sha256` in `cells/111x-pwt-dstar/CELL`.

## Reproducibility

- The published files were written by an x86-64 build with FMA3 (GCC 16.1.0, `-O2 -march=native`). `make` builds the same way (`NATIVE=1`). The tree encoder's model choice and the d\* search use floating point. So byte identity of a rebuild is established for this build only, and for the encoders, not for a rerun of the search. `NATIVE=0` gives a portable build. Every decoder is integer-only and portable.
- Cells 010, 011, 110 and 111 were first written by two older builds of the tree encoder. On 2026-10-06 one build of the current encoder rewrote all four, and the d\* file, byte for byte. Each `CELL` records both binary hashes (`encoder_sha256`, `gate_sha256`). They are machine-specific.
- On the build machine, 15 of the 16 tools built from `src/` are byte-identical to the project binaries that rewrote every published file byte for byte and certified it on 2026-10-06. Among them are `list_build`, `pwt2_encode`, `list_decode`, `cnd_decode` and `pwt2_decode`. `dsel_set2` differs only by the two edits in the next item. The binaries that first wrote the files are older (previous item). The d\* search ran with a 2026-09-24 build of `dsel_set2`.
- `src/` is a snapshot of the project code behind those 2026-10-06 runs. It differs from that code only in comments, a POSIX branch for `dsel_set2`'s memory report, and `dsel_set2`'s default scratch directory (`--scratch` is always passed here).
- A clean copy of this repository, built from `src/` on 2026-10-06, verified all nine files and the oracle (`make verify-CELL`). It rebuilt cells 001 and 101 and the d\* file byte for byte (`make rebuild-CELL`). For the d\* file it used the masks the search saved, which are not hosted (`ROUTE=masks`). It certified cells 001, 101 and 111 (`make certify-CELL`). Its logs are `cells/*/runs/repo_*` and `results/runs/repo-validation-2026-10-06/`. A second clean copy, made the same day for an independent review, verified the same files again and certified 001 and 111. It rebuilt cells 000, 010, 100 and 110 from the oracle alone, with every extraction rerun and each intermediate matching `results/INTERMEDIATES`. It rebuilt the d\* file by the default paths route. All rebuilds matched byte for byte (`results/runs/review-2026-10-06/`).
- Run logs are in `cells/*/runs/` for each cell, `results/runs/` for the shared construction runs, and `oracle/runs/`. They keep the file names in use on the day they were written. Paths are replaced by placeholders. `<repo>` is the project tree in the construction, rebuild and certification logs. In the `repo_*` logs and in `results/runs/repo-validation-2026-10-06/` and `review-2026-10-06/`, it is the clean copy of this repository. `<work>` is the working folder of the runs. `<data>` and `<bin>` are the folders of the data files and the binaries. `<scratch>` and `<tmp>` are scratch folders. `<certified>` holds the certified intermediates. `<toolchain>` is the compiler's folder and `<home>` the user's folder. In `cells/*/expected/`, `<t>` and `<m>` mask times and memory figures, and `<id>` a number that differs from run to run.
- A few logs list more of the project tree than this repository ships. `results/runs/certify-2026-10-06/sources.txt` and `binaries_*.txt` keep only the shipped sources and tools. The `release_data_*` and `stage_release*` files of `results/runs/rebuild-2026-10-06/` predate the final file names and the decision not to host the search masks.

## Layout

```
src/        the tools and headers (C++20, header-only libraries, no dependencies)
tests/      unit tests, the 637 fixture lines, the 10^12 prefix self-test, crafted files
cells/      one folder per cell: CELL manifest, build.sh, decode.sh, expected/, runs/
oracle/     the oracle and the text table: manifests, build.sh, decode.sh
results/    cells.tsv (every number), render.py, comparison.tex, INTERMEDIATES, runs/
docs/       file format specifications, and the website (generated, served by GitHub Pages)
site/       the website generator, its prose and links (cells.json, site.json) and its tests
scripts/    the drivers behind the make targets
```

Formats: [oracle](docs/ORACLE_FORMAT.md), [VByte lists](docs/VBG_FORMAT.md), [residue-class lists](docs/CND_FORMAT.md), [prime wavelet trees](docs/PWT2_FORMAT.md) (built on [an earlier tree format](docs/PWT_FORMAT.md)), [path files](docs/PATHS_FORMAT.md), [search masks](docs/MASKS_FORMAT.md).

The website is built from `results/cells.tsv`, the cell scripts and `site/`. `make site` writes `docs/`, the links block at the top of this README and its Citation block. It also writes the text files of the data folder to `dist/data-folder/`. `make site-check` checks every page and link and runs the site tests.

## Data

The hosted files are lossless encodings of the table of A. Shallue and J. Webster. They are dedicated to the public domain under [CC0 1.0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/). The data folder holds the dedication (`LICENSE-DATA.txt`). The table-derived files in `tests/` (`fixtures/fix_*.txt`, `prefix/prefix_1e12.txt`, `prefix/prefix.orc1` and `prefix/golden_files/`) are data under the same dedication. If you use the data, please cite the table (Shallue and Webster, arXiv:2506.09903) and the paper.
